claim: Purvaiya in Bhojpuri/Purabiya folk song is the easterly wind: Jassal translates 'Jhuruke pavan puruvaiya' as 'Gusts of easterly winds blow', from a song collected at Atra, Jaunpur
source: Smita Tewari Jassal, Unearthing Gender: Folksongs of North India (Duke University Press, 2012; open access)
note: Primary text for the word itself; the song is a woman's lament (husband asleep), so the wind sets a mood in a love-and-separation song. Jaunpur is in the Purabiya/Bhojpuri belt of eastern UP.

claim: Kajari line 'Agan gagan sakhi bahat purvai rama' is translated 'O, dear friend, the Purva wind is blowing'; the authors write the Purva (easterly) wind 'acts as an enemy here': a wind that should comfort pains a woman whose husband is away
value: Purva wind = pain of separation in Kajari
source: Chauhan M. & Mishra S. (IIT BHU) 2024, Kajari Folk Songs: Mechanism for Emotional Regulation, Rupkatha Journal 16(1), doi 10.21659/rupkatha.v16n1.06g
note: Quotes Upadhyay (2020) pp.138-139 for the song line. Peer-reviewed (Web of Science ESCI journal), authors at IIT (BHU) Varanasi.

claim: Monsoon trough on IMD charts runs from Ganganagar to Kolkata passing through Prayagraj; westerly/south-westerly winds lie on its southern side and easterly/south-easterly winds on its northern side; its shifting position governs rainfall distribution
value: trough Ganganagar-Prayagraj-Kolkata; easterlies north of it
source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)
second_source: Gadgil S. (2018) J. Earth Syst. Sci. 127:1, mean July 850 hPa: westerlies south of the trough, easterlies to the north
note: Physical reason (OWN INFERENCE from the IMD line): Bhojpur (Arrah/Buxar/Ballia, about 25 N 84 E) lies on or just north of the Prayagraj-Kolkata trough line, so low-level monsoon air there is easterly/south-easterly, not the south-westerly of Kerala or Mumbai. IMD does not name Bhojpur; the link is ours.

claim: IMD FAQ: in July and August surface winds are westerly/south-westerly south of the monsoon trough and south-easterly/easterly to its north, and are generally stronger over the seas than over land
value: S/SW south of trough; SE/E north of trough
source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon
page_or_section: answer on cyclone-genesis conditions, text line 194 (page number not captured)
note: Independent second IMD statement of the same pattern as claim 03.

claim: NCERT: the Arakan Hills deflect much of the Bay of Bengal branch, so the monsoon enters West Bengal and Bangladesh from the south and south-east, then splits; one branch moves westward along the Ganga plains as far as the Punjab plains
value: Bay branch runs west up the Ganga plain
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate
note: Ledger M042 already holds this; cite M042. A wind moving westward along the plain arrives at Bhojpur as an easterly (own inference); NCERT does not name Bhojpur.

claim: Jassal places her songs in the 'Purabiya and Bhojpuri-speaking countryside of northern India, namely, eastern Uttar Pradesh and western Bihar'
value: Bhojpuri/Purabiya belt = eastern UP + western Bihar
source: Smita Tewari Jassal, Unearthing Gender: Folksongs of North India (Duke University Press, 2012; open access)
note: Gives the cultural region in a university-press source. Jassal does not derive 'Purvaiya' for the wind.

claim: 2011 Census (Table C-16): Bhojpuri is returned by 5,05,79,447 (50,579,447) people, listed among the mother tongues grouped under Hindi
source: Census of India 2011, Paper 1 of 2018, Language: India, States and UTs (Table C-16), Registrar General
page_or_section: Table C-16, Hindi group, row Bhojpuri (text line 280)

claim: ICAR-CRIDA contingency plan for Bhojpur district: normal south-west monsoon (Jun-Sep) rainfall 906 mm over 51 rainy days; normal onset 2nd week of June, normal cessation 2nd week of October; north-east monsoon 58 mm, winter 28 mm
value: 906 mm, 51 days; onset 2nd wk Jun; cessation 2nd wk Oct
source: ICAR-CRIDA, Agriculture Contingency Plan for District Bhojpur (Bihar)
note: Local numbers for the district that names the region. 2013 plan: normals may have moved; no Bhojpur-specific IMD normal in our sources.

claim: Same plan: Bhojpur kharif rice area 82.3 thousand ha, production 155.3 thousand tonnes, yield 1,885 kg/ha; normal sowing window for irrigated kharif rice is 3rd week of June to 4th week of July; canals supply 60.6% of irrigated area
value: 82.3 th ha; 155.3 th t; sowing 3rd wk Jun - 4th wk Jul
source: ICAR-CRIDA, Agriculture Contingency Plan for District Bhojpur (Bihar)
note: Farming-calendar anchor: rice sowing/transplanting follows monsoon onset.

claim: NCERT traditional Indian seasons: Varsha (rains) is Sravana-Bhadra, July-August; Sharada is Asvina-Kartika, September-October
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate
note: Sawan = Sravana: the month the Kajari and swing songs are named for. NCERT gives approximate Gregorian months.

claim: Jassal: in the agricultural cycle the rainy season is when farm activity is slowest, making it the ideal time for wives to spend a couple of months with their natal families (a leave won by 'coaxing and cajoling' in song)
source: Smita Tewari Jassal, Unearthing Gender: Folksongs of North India (Duke University Press, 2012; open access)
note: Fieldwork in Jaunpur villages at monsoon onset. Paraphrase; concerns women's work cycle and sits in tension with the paddy-transplanting rush (claim 12).

claim: Jaunpur paddy-transplanting work song: 'Rimi jhimi barase la paniya, ava cali dhan ropai dhaniya', translated 'It's raining, let's go transplant paddy'
source: Smita Tewari Jassal, Unearthing Gender: Folksongs of North India (Duke University Press, 2012; open access)
note: Shows the farming calendar in song: the rain sets the work.

claim: Jassal links the Kajli (Kajari) genre to women's monsoon frolic: chances to laugh, joke and trade banter; a Kajari song in the book has the line 'kajariya khelei javai re naiharavā' (going to play Kajari at the natal home)
value: Kajari = women's monsoon play, natal visits
source: Smita Tewari Jassal, Unearthing Gender: Folksongs of North India (Duke University Press, 2012; open access)
page_or_section: ch.3 conclusion, pp.149-150; song text about p.103
note: Cultural link between monsoon, Sawan, natal-home visits and swings (a verse in the same book names 'kajri malhar' sung on the swing).

claim: Kajari is a folk genre sung mainly by women in Sawan (north Indian monsoon, July-August); the authors write 'it is believed' that the dark clouds prompted women and men to sing; the word relates to kajal (kohl); prevalent in eastern Uttar Pradesh and some parts of Bihar
source: Chauhan M. & Mishra S. (IIT BHU) 2024, Kajari Folk Songs: Mechanism for Emotional Regulation, Rupkatha Journal 16(1), doi 10.21659/rupkatha.v16n1.06g
note: Audit fix: the dark-clouds origin is the authors' hedged belief ('It is believed that'), not a finding. The authors cite Jassal (2012) only for the definition of the genre.

claim: Chauhan and Mishra, citing Singh (2016): migration 'gave birth to distinct folk culture' in the Bhojpuri region; Biraha (sung by the Ahir community), Bidesiya and Kajari are among its most popular genres
source: Chauhan M. & Mishra S. (IIT BHU) 2024, Kajari Folk Songs: Mechanism for Emotional Regulation, Rupkatha Journal 16(1), doi 10.21659/rupkatha.v16n1.06g
note: Secondary claim by the authors, not checked at Singh (2016). The same page links colonial-era labour recruitment after 1833 to the region; keep that out of the video unless a history source is added.

claim: Most Kajari songs name migration destinations ('pardes' or 'bides'): Mirzapur, Bengal, Rangoon, Braj, Mathura appear in songs; the authors read Sawan as aggravating the loneliness of left-behind wives
source: Chauhan M. & Mishra S. (IIT BHU) 2024, Kajari Folk Songs: Mechanism for Emotional Regulation, Rupkatha Journal 16(1), doi 10.21659/rupkatha.v16n1.06g
page_or_section: pp.4-5 of 19 (destinations); p.12 of 19 (Sawan aggravating loneliness)
note: Links the season's wind to the migration ethos.

claim: Authors' reading of Kajari imagery: the same rain and clouds that give life to millions of peasants in the Bhojpuri region 'function as an enemy' for left-behind women; cuckoo and peacock calls and the cool breeze also turn painful
value: rain = boon for fields, pain for separated women
source: Chauhan M. & Mishra S. (IIT BHU) 2024, Kajari Folk Songs: Mechanism for Emotional Regulation, Rupkatha Journal 16(1), doi 10.21659/rupkatha.v16n1.06g
note: Gives the double-edged ethos point: the monsoon as blessing and ache.

claim: Sangeet Natak Akademi annual report 2016-17 records a 'Special Documentation of Bhojpuri Songs' by Smt. Pushpa Prasad (eminent folk singer of Bihar) at Meghdoot Theatre, New Delhi, 20 Aug 2016
source: Sangeet Natak Akademi, Annual Report 2016-2017
page_or_section: section 'Special documentation of Bhojpuri songs by Smt. Pushpa Prasad'
note: Official recognition of Bhojpuri song only. It does NOT mention the monsoon, Kajari or Purvaiya, so it cannot back the wind-culture link.
